questions.q: What does PARTITION BY do in the ROW_NUMBER() example?
options: Groups rows sharing the same values in specified columns, like GROUP BY but without collapsing rows
Deletes rows immediately
Sorts the entire table by one column
Filters out NULL values only
questions.explain: PARTITION BY defines the groups ROW_NUMBER() numbers within, without reducing the row count like GROUP BY would.

questions.q: What does a RowNum value greater than 1 signal for a given group?
options: That row is a duplicate of an earlier row in the same PARTITION BY group
That row has a NULL value somewhere
That row is the original, unique row
Nothing — RowNum has no practical meaning
questions.explain: Since RowNum starts at 1 and counts up within each group, anything beyond 1 is, by definition, a repeat.

questions.q: Why should you always run the SELECT version of a duplicate-finding query before converting it to a DELETE?
options: DELETE is a genuinely destructive operation, and reviewing which rows match first avoids removing the wrong data
SELECT and DELETE must always be run together in the same statement
SQL Server requires a SELECT to run before every DELETE automatically
It has no real safety benefit — this is purely a stylistic habit
questions.explain: This is a core safety practice — confirm exactly which rows will be affected before doing something irreversible.

questions.q: In the DELETE example, which copy of each duplicate group survives?
options: The one with the lowest value per the ORDER BY inside OVER (e.g. lowest BusinessEntityID)
A randomly chosen row from the group
The most recently inserted row
All copies are deleted, leaving nothing
questions.explain: RowNum = 1 goes to whichever row sorts first per the ORDER BY clause inside OVER(), and that row is excluded from the DELETE.

questions.q: What real-world scenario commonly causes duplicate rows to appear in a table?
options: A form submitted twice, or an import/sync process run more than once without proper deduplication
Duplicates never occur in real, well-designed databases
Only GROUP BY queries can produce duplicate rows
Duplicates only happen when using CHAR instead of VARCHAR
questions.explain: This is a genuinely common real-world data-quality problem, which is why this deduplication technique matters in practice.
